rubric.why: Identifies nutrition as a process involving obtaining and using food.
rubric.description: Nutrition is a process of obtaining and using food.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing nutrition as a process of obtaining and using food.

rubric.why: States a purpose for using food.
rubric.description: Food is used for energy, growth, repair or maintenance.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving at least one valid purpose of food.

modelAnswer: Nutrition is the process by which organisms obtain food and use it for energy, growth, repair and maintenance of the body.

items.followUp: Write two functions of the stem in plants.

rubric.why: Recognizes the root’s role in taking up water and minerals or anchoring the plant.
rubric.description: Roots absorb water and mineral salts from the soil and/or anchor the plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either absorption or anchorage.

rubric.why: Gives another valid root function.
rubric.description: Roots may store food and/or help support the plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a second valid function, such as food storage or support.

modelAnswer: Roots absorb water and mineral salts from the soil.
Roots anchor the plant in the soil and may also store food.

items.followUp: Differentiate between a source and a sink in the transport of food in plants.

rubric.why: Identifies a source as a part that supplies food for transport.
rubric.description: A source produces or releases sugars for transport, commonly a photosynthesizing leaf.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the source as the food-producing or food-releasing part.

rubric.why: Identifies a sink as a part that uses or stores transported food.
rubric.description: A sink uses or stores sugars, such as a growing or non-photosynthetic part.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the sink as a food-using or food-storing part.

modelAnswer: A source is a plant part, usually a photosynthesizing leaf, that produces or releases sugars for transport.
A sink is a plant part that uses or stores the sugars transported to it.

items.followUp: Name the three formed elements of blood.

rubric.why: Gives the number of main blood cell types/formed elements.
rubric.description: There are three main types of formed elements in blood.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that there are three types.

rubric.why: Names at least two types of blood cells/formed elements.
rubric.description: Names any two: red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming any two correct types.

modelAnswer: There are three main types of formed elements in blood: red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.
Any two are: red blood cells and white blood cells.

items.followUp: Describe the difference between tissue-level and organ-level organization.

rubric.why: Defines unicellular organization by the single cell performing life processes.
rubric.description: A unicellular organism consists of one cell that carries out all life functions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that one cell performs the organism’s life functions.

rubric.why: Describes multicellular organisms as having many, often specialized, cells.
rubric.description: A multicellular organism has many cells, often specialized for different functions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it has many cells, with specialization as supporting detail.

rubric.why: Identifies colonial organization as a group of cells living together.
rubric.description: A colonial organism is a group of similar cells living together.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing a colony as a group of cells.

rubric.why: Distinguishes a colony from a fully integrated multicellular organism.
rubric.description: In a colony, cells generally retain considerable independence and may perform life functions individually.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting that colonial cells retain independence or can function individually.

modelAnswer: In unicellular organization, an organism consists of a single cell that performs all life functions.
In multicellular organization, an organism consists of many cells, which may be specialized for different functions.
In colonial organization, a group of similar cells lives together in a colony.
The cells of a colony generally retain considerable independence and may perform life functions individually.

items.followUp: Describe the structure and functions of the epidermis and cortex in a plant root.

rubric.why: Names the principal conducting elements of xylem.
rubric.description: Xylem includes vessels and tracheids; its conducting elements are generally dead and have thickened walls.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming vessels or tracheids as xylem elements.

rubric.why: States what xylem transports.
rubric.description: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from roots to the rest of the plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that xylem transports water and mineral salts.

rubric.why: Names the principal phloem components.
rubric.description: Phloem consists mainly of sieve tubes and companion cells; sieve tubes are living conducting cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming sieve tubes or companion cells as phloem components.

rubric.why: States what phloem transports.
rubric.description: Phloem transports sugars and other organic food substances.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that phloem transports sugars or food.

rubric.why: Adds the direction or route of phloem translocation.
rubric.description: Food is translocated from sources to sinks and may move in either direction through the plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating source-to-sink movement or bidirectional transport.

modelAnswer: Xylem is made up mainly of vessels and tracheids; these conducting elements are generally dead and have thickened walls.
Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to the rest of the plant.
Phloem consists mainly of sieve tubes and companion cells; sieve tubes are living conducting cells.
Phloem transports sugars and other organic food substances from sources to sinks.
Phloem transport may occur in either direction, according to the locations of the sources and sinks.

items.followUp: Explain how pH and enzyme concentration affect the rate of enzyme action.

rubric.why: Explains that warming initially increases enzyme activity up to an optimum.
rubric.description: As temperature rises, enzyme action generally increases up to an optimum temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the rise in rate up to the optimum.

rubric.why: Explains the effect of excessive temperature.
rubric.description: Above the optimum, the enzyme may denature, changing its active site and reducing the reaction rate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that high temperature denatures the enzyme or lowers its activity.

rubric.why: Explains the initial effect of increasing substrate concentration.
rubric.description: Increasing substrate concentration increases the rate because more enzyme-substrate complexes form.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking more substrate to a higher rate or more enzyme-substrate complexes.

rubric.why: Explains why the rate stops increasing at high substrate concentration.
rubric.description: Once enzyme active sites are saturated, the rate reaches a maximum and does not rise further unless more enzyme is added.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning saturation, occupied active sites or a maximum rate.

modelAnswer: As temperature rises, the rate of enzyme action generally increases until the enzyme reaches its optimum temperature.
Above the optimum temperature, the enzyme may denature; its active site changes shape and the rate falls.
Increasing substrate concentration increases the rate because more enzyme-substrate complexes can form.
At high substrate concentration, all active sites become occupied; the enzyme is saturated and the rate reaches a maximum.

items.followUp: State four ways in which fertilizers help crop plants.

rubric.why: Identifies fertilizers as a source of essential mineral nutrients.
rubric.description: Fertilizers supply essential mineral nutrients, such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that fertilizers supply mineral nutrients or giving suitable examples.

rubric.why: Explains that fertilizers replenish soil nutrients removed by crops.
rubric.description: They restore nutrients depleted from the soil by plant growth and harvesting.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing replenishment or replacement of soil nutrients.

rubric.why: States that nutrients support plant growth.
rubric.description: They promote healthy vegetative and root growth.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid growth benefit.

rubric.why: States a crop-production benefit.
rubric.description: They can increase crop yield and improve agricultural production.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that fertilizers increase yield or production.

modelAnswer: Fertilizers supply essential mineral nutrients, such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
They replenish nutrients depleted from the soil by plant growth and harvesting.
The added nutrients promote healthy plant growth.
Fertilizers can increase crop yield and agricultural production.
